newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. official ends term worried over peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official ends term worried over peace.

text.p: U.S. Jerusalem Consul-General Edward Abington, who ends his assignment this week, said on Monday he was leaving with great sorrow and deep concern over the future of deadlocked Middle East peace moves.
Abington, a 54-year-old red-headed Texan, said he would leave on Thursday after four years of intensive involvement in trying to resolve the Israeli-Arab conflict.
"It's been a very extraordinarily intensive and very emotional experience," Abington told Reuters.
"I leave here with a real feeling of sadness and deep concern about where the peace process is and where it's going to be," he said.

PLO-Israel peace moves have been deadlocked since March when Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, sparking Palestinian street protests. U.S. mediation efforts have failed to restart the talks.

Western diplomats said Abington, who represents Washington in Jerusalem and who become Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's confidant, had been at odds with American ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk over U.S. policy issues.
The dispute partly concerns which U.S. office represents the United States in Jerusalem, the city which is perhaps the most difficult issue at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian dispute.
The U.S. Consulate General in Jerusalem is independent of the U.S. embassy in Tel Aviv and reports directly to the State Department.
The Consul-General is Washington's designated political conduit to the Palestinian Authority while the U.S. Ambassador's "distinct reporting area" is Israel.
At times, Abington made daily trips from Jerusalem to Arafat's headquarters in self-ruled Gaza at different times of the day and night to help resolve Israeli-PLO deadlock.
Abington said since he was closely involved in times of crisis and peacemaking with the Palestinians and Israelis, "no foreign diplomat has become closer to Arafat than I have."

Indyk, once affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the main pro-Israel U.S. Jewish lobby, who is also ending his assignment in Israel, will be promoted to the position of Assistant Secretary of State on Middle East and other issues.

Diplomats said that Abington, however, who has been critical of Israeli policies towards the Palestinians, faces an uncertain position at the State Department and will be distanced from Middle East issues.
"I feel very fortunate in playing a role in representing the U.S. during this four-year period," Abington said.

"I remember during the Palestinian elections, Palestinians had such a tremendous feeling of pride. I'll never forget an elderly woman going to vote. She was crying. I asked her why and she said she never voted before," he said. "I was deeply touched by that."

"But Palestinians still have a long way to go. It's very difficult now. Violence is deeply troubling, but sooner or later the process will go back on track because there is no alternative but to continue the peace process," he added.
